clue.text: Outlaw gang with appeal

indicators.note: with means one piece comes along beside the other, placed straight after it

blocks.note: a band is a group or gang of people
it is old slang for sex appeal, as in the it girl

explanation.surface: A criminal mob with charm and charisma, like a Robin Hood band.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for appeal comes from the 1920s phrase for sex appeal; crosswords use it often.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandit is a robber living beyond the law, so the two nouns are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Second shot rebounded

blocks.note: to second a motion is to back it
fired, as a gun is shot

explanation.surface: A second shot bounced back off a target.
explanation.walkthrough: Second looks like a number or a moment; it is the verb meaning to support.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that backfired went wrong and hurt its maker, just as something that rebounded came back on them.

clue.text: On the fence to see astonishing late run

indicators.note: something astonishing is wild and surprising, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the seven letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: A spectator sits on a fence to watch a surprising last-minute sprint.
explanation.walkthrough: On the fence is an idiom for not taking sides, not a place to sit.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sitting on the fence refuses to back either party, which is the impartial stance of a non-aligned onlooker.

clue.text: Gremlin fliers found on take-off initially responsible for damage?

indicators.note: found on means set beside, so this part follows straight after
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: a gremlin is a mischievous imp
airmen fly aircraft
first letter of take-off

explanation.surface: Pilots blame gremlins for a fault that appears as their plane takes off.
explanation.walkthrough: Gremlins were RAF folklore, imps said to sabotage aircraft, which makes the picture of mischief fit the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Impairment is the weakening or harming of something, so it is a form of harm done to a machine or body.

clue.text: Type of cap for a prison officer?

definitions.note: a hat belonging to a warder: in slang a screw's top

blocks.note: first meaning: a lid with a thread that twists onto a jar or bottle
second meaning, whimsical: the headwear of a warder, who in British slang is a screw

explanation.walkthrough: Screw is British slang for a prison warder, so the warder's headgear would be his top; read normally it is a jar lid.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw-top is a lid with a thread, twisted on to close a bottle or jar.

clue.text: Firm implant for treatment of illness

indicators.note: for treatment means the letters are worked on and handled into a new form

blocks.note: Co is short for company, a firm
the letters of implant rearranged

explanation.surface: A medical company makes an implant to treat a disease.
explanation.walkthrough: Treatment sits naturally in the medical scene, but it signals rearranging the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint is a medical ailment, as in a chest complaint, so it means a disorder of the body.

clue.text: Feather nest to accommodate bird

indicators.note: the two words accommodate the answer, holding it within their run of letters

blocks.note: found inside the letters of feather nest

explanation.surface: A bird lines its nest with feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: Feather looks like a noun; it is the verb, to line with feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, a crossword regular among large birds of prey.

clue.text: Express in one of the main stations, perhaps

blocks.note: to term something is to name or express it
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An express train pulls into one of the big city stations.
explanation.walkthrough: Express sounds like a fast train in this railway scene; it is the verb to put into words.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminus is the end station of a line, and big city rail hubs are often such end points.

clue.text: A bit of floral decoration in a ring round shirt

indicators.note: round means the ring goes all the way about the other letter

blocks.note: a peal is a ring of bells
a T-shirt, shortened to its letter

explanation.surface: A shirt printed with a flower pattern inside a circle.
explanation.walkthrough: Ring suggests a circle or jewellery, but it is the sound of bells.
explanation.definitionFit: A single coloured leaf of a flower is one small part of a bloom used to adorn things.

clue.text: Goddess getting hard time

blocks.note: H for hard, as on pencils
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A goddess going through a tough patch.
explanation.walkthrough: Hard time reads as a single phrase, but the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Hera is the Greek queen of the gods, wife of Zeus, a deity of marriage and women.

clue.text: Representative in vineyard with the French founder

indicators.note: with tells us the last piece simply joins on at the end

blocks.note: a cru is a French vineyard or its wine, as in grand cru
a Member of Parliament represents a constituency
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A politician visiting a wine estate alongside a French company founder.
explanation.walkthrough: Founder looks like a noun, a person who sets up a business; here it is the verb meaning to collapse or sink.
explanation.definitionFit: To founder is to give way and collapse, and to crumple is likewise to fold up and give way.

clue.text: Weapon covering retreat of gunners followed by tank leader from turret

indicators.note: a retreat goes back the way it came, so the gunners' letters run backwards
the weapon covers something by wrapping round it
followed by puts the next piece straight after what has been built
the leader of a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: a mine is an explosive weapon
RA, the Royal Artillery, written backwards
first letter of tank

explanation.surface: A war scene: a weapon covers gunners pulling back, while a tank commander emerges from its turret.
explanation.walkthrough: Turret looks like part of the tank picture, but it is the definition: a minaret is a slender tower on a mosque. RA is the Royal Artillery, the British army's gunners.
explanation.definitionFit: A turret is a small tower, and a minaret is the tall slender tower of a mosque.

clue.text: Possible to cross water submerging motorway, but it's dangerous

indicators.note: a river crossing that submerges something holds it inside, under the water
to means attached to, so the first word joins on after what follows

blocks.note: to ford is to wade across a river
the M1, Britain's main north-south motorway, written with I for 1
able means capable, possible to do

explanation.surface: It's possible to wade across where flood water covers the motorway, but it's risky.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds; crosswords write it MI. ABLE comes first in the clue but goes last in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Formidable means inspiring fear because of strength or power, so a formidable thing is one that poses a threat.

clue.text: Female student outfit rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the outfit word runs backwards

blocks.note: a rig is a set of clothes or kit
L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A young woman at college has her clothes turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: Student comes first in the clue but its letter goes last.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl is a young woman, so the noun female covers her as a general term for a woman.

clue.text: Restriction on horse fair during bad weather

indicators.note: during means within a span, so the fair goes inside the stormy weather

blocks.note: a mart is a market or fair, followed by in
a gale is a strong wind

explanation.surface: A horse fair is called off because of a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: MART is a market; IN comes from during, which here puts the fair in the time of the gale.
explanation.definitionFit: A martingale is a strap from noseband or reins to girth that stops a horse throwing its head up.

clue.text: Sponge served after bread in fishy delicacy

indicators.note: served after means this part is placed behind the other one

blocks.note: a roll is a small loaf of bread
to mop is to soak up liquid, like a sponge

explanation.surface: A dinner course: sponge pudding brought out after the bread rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: Sponge suggests a cake, but it is a verb here, to soak up.
explanation.definitionFit: A rollmop is a pickled herring fillet rolled round onion, a cold dish of fish often eaten as a treat.

clue.text: Exercises expected to absorb keen teacher

indicators.note: to absorb is to soak up and hold within, so one word goes inside another

blocks.note: PE is physical education, school exercises
due means expected, as a train is due
agog means eager, keen

explanation.surface: A keen teacher is expected to soak up physical training.
explanation.walkthrough: Exercises sounds like the teacher's workouts, but here it is just the school subject abbreviation, PE, for physical education.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedagogue is a schoolmaster, often a strict or pedantic one; the word is formal for an instructor.

clue.text: "..extant and written in very choice (Hamlet)

blocks.note: surface reading: an unfinished quotation, with its last word blanked out on the printed page
setter's reading: Hamlet's line about the play-within-the-play, whose story is extant and written in a choice language

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet, Act 3, says of the poisoning play: 'The story is extant, and written in very choice' and then names the language. The printed clue has a blank where that word goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Shakespeare's line names the language of Rome and Florence that the old story was written in.

clue.text: Confident monarch boarding new vessel on voyage

indicators.note: boarding means getting on and going inside, so the monarch goes into the vessel
a voyage moves things about, so the vessel's letters are shifted

blocks.note: N for new
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
the letters of vessel rearranged

explanation.surface: The Queen boards a new ship and sets out on a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen's cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerveless can mean cool and fearless, showing no nerves, so it is calm and sure of oneself.

clue.text: Tom-tit was kept by doctor

definitions.note: a cryptic hint: Tom, the little chimney sweep of Kingsley's The Water-Babies, was drowned

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two parts sit side by side

blocks.note: Dr is the usual abbreviation for doctor
something kept is possessed, held as one's own

explanation.surface: A little bird kept as a pet by a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom-tit is not the bird but a tiny Tom: the sweep in Charles Kingsley's The Water-Babies falls into a river and drowns, becoming a water-baby.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Victorian children's story the small hero dies in the water, so what befell him fits the past participle.

clue.text: Casual worker has bad start

indicators.note: start says this part comes first, at the beginning

blocks.note: off means gone bad, like sour milk
a hand is a labourer, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A temporary employee makes a poor beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: Casual worker reads as one phrase, a temp; casual is the definition and worker a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An offhand manner is careless and unceremonious, which is the relaxed, informal sense of casual.

clue.text: Honorary workers in trial broadcast

indicators.note: in places the workers inside the other set of letters
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of trial are strewn about

blocks.note: TU is a trade union, a body of workers
the letters of trial rearranged

explanation.surface: Unpaid staff take part in a court case that is shown on television.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadcast suggests radio or TV, but here it means scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: A titular post is held in name only, carrying a title without real duties or pay, much like an honorary one.

clue.text: Beastly accommodation for neat occupants, perhaps

definitions.note: a description: lodging meant for cattle

blocks.note: first meaning: housing for beasts, not nasty lodgings
second meaning: pens whose occupants are cattle, neat being an old word for oxen

explanation.walkthrough: Neat looks like tidy, but it is an archaic word for cattle; beastly means for beasts, not nasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Lairage is the pens where cattle are kept at a market or abattoir before sale or slaughter.

clue.text: Abandoned port

blocks.note: first meaning: gone away from, deserted
second meaning: the side of a ship on the ... when facing forward

explanation.surface: A harbour town that has been deserted.
explanation.walkthrough: Port looks like a harbour; it is the sailor's word for the left-hand side.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the past tense of leave, meaning deserted, and the side a sailor calls port.

clue.text: Book right off shelf

indicators.note: off means taken away, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: a ledger is an account book
R for right

explanation.surface: Taking a book off the shelf on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: Right looks like a direction to the shelf; it is the letter to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: A ledge is a narrow flat projection from a wall, used like a shelf to rest things on.

clue.text: A Governor-general negotiating rise and increase in power

indicators.note: negotiating means working round or through, so these letters are worked into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
GG is the standard abbreviation for Governor-General
the seven letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: A colonial governor bargains his way up and gains more authority.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'rise and'; the copy here misread it as 'rise 2nd'. A Governor-General represents the Crown in Commonwealth countries such as Canada.
explanation.definitionFit: To aggrandise is to make greater in rank, wealth or influence, which is to boost someone's standing and might.

clue.text: Sent under cover reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard said, so we go by sound and not spelling

blocks.note: something under cover is wrapped up

explanation.surface: A parcel posted in disguise, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: Sent looks like posted; it means sent into raptures, delighted.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sent is slang for being carried away with joy, and rapt describes that enchanted, absorbed state.

clue.text: Type of airman getting little money on way up?

indicators.note: getting means taking on, so the next piece is added after
in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the whole is backwards

blocks.note: AC1, aircraftman first class, the lowest RAF rank, with I for 1
p for penny or pence

explanation.surface: What kind of serviceman is paid so little as he climbs the ranks?
explanation.walkthrough: AC1 is Aircraftman First Class, a junior RAF rank. Type is printing type; pica is a type size.
explanation.definitionFit: Pica is a printing measure and the name of a typeface size, twelve points, used on typewriters.

clue.text: Pull round to secure victory - or getting a tie?

indicators.note: round means the pulling word goes all the way about the other piece

blocks.note: to drag is to pull
to win is to secure a victory

explanation.surface: A team strives to win but may end level.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the joke: you can win or draw, and the answer is made by putting a win inside a drag.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawn game ends level, so a side heading for that result is finishing all square with the other side.

clue.text: Calm current in American river

indicators.note: in places the current inside the river's letters

blocks.note: the River Plate, between Argentina and Uruguay in South America
AC is alternating current

explanation.surface: A gentle flow of water in a river in the Americas.
explanation.walkthrough: Calm and current both suggest water, but calm is a verb and current is electrical. American covers South America too, home of the River Plate.
explanation.definitionFit: To placate someone is to soothe their anger, making them quiet and settled again.

clue.text: Made attractive design to include expensive eastern components

indicators.note: to include means the design word holds the other parts inside it

blocks.note: an end is an aim or purpose, a design
dear means costly
E for eastern, the last of the components put inside

explanation.surface: A designer makes a room appealing using costly oriental parts.
explanation.walkthrough: Design looks like a drawing; here it is an aim, as in by design. The D of END stays at the far end.
explanation.definitionFit: To endear is to make someone loved or liked, so the past tense describes having made a person charming to others.

clue.text: Headgear for engineers involved in risks

indicators.note: involved in means caught up inside, so the engineers go within the risks

blocks.note: a bet is a gamble, a risk
RE is the Royal Engineers, the British army's engineering corps

explanation.surface: Hard hats protect engineers in dangerous jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: Headgear suggests safety helmets, but the hats are soft military caps.
explanation.definitionFit: A beret is a round flat cap of soft felt, worn by soldiers among others, so it is a kind of hat.
